newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Re-election drive seen dominating week in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Re-election drive seen dominating week in Brazil.

text.p: The Brazilian goverment will concentrate this week on mustering support in the Chamber of Deputies for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's 1998 re-election dream, congressional officials said.
"There's going to be a lot of meetings and a lot of talking," said a government source in Congress who asked not to be named.

Other key legislation was on the agenda, like a new agricultural tax aimed at reducing concentration of land ownership. But rewriting the constitution to permit re-election would be top of the government's agenda, the source said.

A constitutional amendment allowing Cardoso, as well as sitting state governors and mayors, to stand for a second term is expected to be put to the first of two votes in the lower house in mid-January.
Constitutional amendments require two three-fifths majorities in both houses of Congress. In the Chamber of Deputies, a three-fifths majority is equivalent to 308 votes.
The source said he believed reports that between 275 and 295 deputies had declared themselves in favor of the amendment which is currently at committee level.
Cardoso was due to continue meeting with lawmakers as part of a campaign to win over at least 340 members of the lower house before the amendment was put a vote on the floor of the chamber, he said.

The negotiations were not likely to be affected by an ongoing investigation into an alleged corruption scandal involving the leader of the government-allied Brazilian Labor Party (PTB), the source added.
Dep. Pedrinho Abrao has been under investigation since last week when a newspaper alleged he demanded a bribe from a construction company in return for approval of a dam project.
Newspapers on Monday said it was likely that Abrao, who has denied the allegation, would be stripped of his mandate.
The most important bill due to be put to a vote this week in the Chamber of Deputies would raise a tax charged on unused arable land and give the state more powers to confiscate such properties.
The bill is considered the boldest step taken so far by the government in its attempts to address the issue of land reform, which has so far been blocked in Congress by a strong landowners' lobby.
Brazil has one of the world's most unequal land distribution ratios with an estimated 44 percent of farmland in the hands of just one percent of landowners.
Land reform was also likely to be on the agenda in the upper house with a Thursday vote seen for a bill which would speed up Brazil's land reform procedure.

The Senate was also due to vote on a bill setting new corporate tax rules, mainly to close a loophole exploited by multinational firms, and on legislation to regulate the opening up to foreigners of Brazil's inland and coastal shipping sector.
